title: 道德經 第二十六章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 26, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 65. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 26 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 重德 (The Potency of Weight). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
重為輕根，
靜為躁君。

morph.gloss: the heavy, weight (zhòng; chóng is 'again, a layer')
the light, what has no weight
restless, jumpy — the graph carries a foot in it, fidgeting that will not keep still

sentences.l:
The heavy is the root of the light,
the still is the lord of the restless.
sentences.n: Chinese has no verb 'to be' (chapter 1), so where a copula is really wanted, 為 'act as, count as' stands in for it: 'the heavy serves as root to the light'. The couplet is the whole chapter, and both halves are political — 根 the root a plant cannot leave, 君 the lord a subject cannot do without. The traditional chapter title, 重德, reads 重 'weight' as the potency at issue.

sentences.t: 是以聖人終日行不離輜重。

morph.gloss: therefore, for this reason — literally 'by this'
the sage — in this book the ruler who holds the Way, not a holy man
to the end of, right through
to travel, to be on the march (xíng)
to part from, to get away from
the baggage train — the covered supply wagons that trail an army

sentences.l: Therefore the sage travels the whole day through and does not leave the baggage-wagons.
sentences.i: So the sage is on the road all day and never gets away from his baggage-carts.
sentences.n: 輜重 is a soldier's word: the slow covered wagons carrying an army's stores, the thing a commander must never outrun. Its second character is 重, the 'heavy' of the line above — the sage on the march keeps his weight with him. Some witnesses read 君子, 'the gentleman', for 聖人 'the sage': a smaller and more Confucian figure, and a reminder that this chapter is addressed to men with armies.

sentences.t:
雖有榮觀，
燕處超然。

morph.gloss: in glory, in flower — the character is a tree in blossom
a lookout tower on a palace wall — read guàn, the building; guān is the verb 'to gaze' you met in chapter 1
at ease, in comfort — the graph is a swallow, written here for the word 宴/晏 'ease'
to dwell, to take up one's place (chǔ, the verb; chù is 'a place')
clear above it all, holding aloof — 超 'to vault over' with 然 turning it into a manner
to leap over, to pass beyond
so, thus — makes a manner of the word before it

sentences.l:
Though he has towers in their glory,
he dwells at ease, holding clear above.
sentences.i: Splendid towers may be his; he lives at ease and holds himself clear above them.
sentences.n: Two decisions in one line. 觀 may be the verb 'to gaze' (榮觀 = 'glorious sights') or the noun 'a watchtower' (榮觀 = 'towers in their splendour'); we take the noun, because 燕處 beside it is a dwelling and the sentence is about what a ruler owns. And 燕 is a swallow — the bird — written here for a different word altogether, 'ease, feasting', which sounded like it. Old Chinese does this constantly; you met it in chapter 9, where 梲 stood for 銳 'to sharpen'.

sentences.t:
奈何萬乘之主，
而以身輕天下？
輕則失本，
躁則失君。

morph.gloss: how could it be that —? — a fixed question, literally 'do what about?'
to deal with, to do about
ten thousand chariots — the standing measure of a first-rank state, and so a name for its ruler; 乘 is read shèng, a chariot with its team, not chéng 'to ride'
a war-chariot and its four horses (shèng)
his own person — body and self at once
to make light of — the adjective 'light' now a transitive verb
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it
the root, the base — 木 'tree' with a stroke marking its foot
the lordship, the place of the one in charge

sentences.l:
How is it that the lord of ten-thousand chariots
should yet, with his own person, make light of all-under-heaven?
Light — then the root is lost;
restless — then the lordship is lost.
sentences.i: How can the lord of ten thousand chariots let his own person make light of all under heaven? Be light and you lose your root; be restless and you lose your lordship.
sentences.n: 輕 was an adjective two lines ago and is a verb here, 'to make light of'; nothing marks the change but where it stands. The middle line is genuinely disputed. Read 以身 as 'with his own person' — the reading printed here — and it says the ruler puts his own weight into treating all under heaven lightly; read it as 'for his person's sake' and it says he makes light of all under heaven in order to indulge himself; a third reading takes 輕 comparatively — he holds himself lighter than all under heaven. Wang Bi's comment is brief — the light cannot steady the heavy, and to lose the root is to lose oneself — which favours the first. The last two lines take back the chapter's opening words: 本 'root' answers 根, and 君 answers 君.
